# Genesis 48: Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

This chapter records Jacob's deathbed adoption and blessing of Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. In doing so, Jacob grants Joseph the double portion of the firstborn, elevates the younger Ephraim above the elder Manasseh, and pronounces a blessing that becomes a lasting formula in Israel. Hebrews 11:21 highlights this as an act of faith: "By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff."

---

## v. 1: "Some time later Joseph was told, 'Your father is ill.' So he set out with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim."

- The previous chapter ended with Jacob bowed on his bed; now his death is drawing closer. Joseph takes his two sons so that they may see and be blessed by their grandfather before he dies. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- Ellicott notes the chapter's purpose: to settle the matter of who would be heads of "families" (tribes) in Israel, and only Jacob's authority as patriarch could bestow two tribes upon Joseph. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Manasseh and Ephraim were roughly 18–20 years old at this point, having been born before the famine (cf. Genesis 41:50). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 2: "When Jacob was told, 'Your son Joseph has come to you,' Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed."

- The change from "Jacob" to "Israel" is significant. Jacob, enfeebled with age, gathered his strength to act as *Israel* — the bearer of the covenant promises, the prince with God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch: "Jacob, enfeebled with age, gathered up his strength for a work, which he was about to perform as Israel, the bearer of the grace of the promise." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Dr. Constable: "It was as Israel, the prince with God, that Jacob performed this official and significant act." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 3: "Jacob said to Joseph, 'God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there He blessed me.'"

- "God Almighty" is *El Shaddai*. Jacob grounds the adoption of Joseph's sons in the covenant promise God gave him at Bethel (Genesis 35:9–12). This is the same covenant name by which God revealed Himself to Abraham (Genesis 17:1). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- The use of the old name "Luz" instead of "Bethel" shows how slowly old Canaanite place-names gave way to new Hebrew names. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Enduring Word: Jacob vividly remembered this encounter with God; Abraham was careful to pass down the exact words of the covenant. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

---

## v. 4: "'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you; I will make you a multitude of peoples, and will give this land to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession.'"

- The phrasing echoes the promises to Abraham in Genesis 17:2, 6, 8. The exact words of God's covenant were preserved and handed down faithfully. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- Ellicott: In Genesis 35:11 the words are "a congregation of nations"; here "a congregation of peoples" (same Hebrew word *qahal*). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Constable: "Jacob may be losing his health, but he is not losing his memory." He recalls in detail the promises of fertility, multiplication, an assembly of nations, and the land. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 5: "'And now your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.'"

- This is a formal adoption. Jacob elevates Joseph's two sons to the status of his own first- and second-born. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Reformed / Calvin (via Ligonier):** Since God promised Jacob a multitude of descendants, Jacob possessed the authority to incorporate Joseph's sons, who were born outside his household in Egypt, into the number of his own heirs. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Ellicott: "Ephraim shall be regarded as my firstborn, and Manasseh as my second son." 1 Chronicles 5:2 confirms: "though Judah prevailed above his brethren… yet the birthright was Joseph's." The double portion of the firstborn was given to Joseph by granting him two tribes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Enduring Word / Guzik: Ephraim and Manasseh functioned as "replacements" for Reuben and Simeon, who had disqualified themselves through sin (Reuben in Genesis 35:22; Simeon and Levi in Genesis 34:25). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** This adoption illustrates the superiority of faith's vision over what men see naturally. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 6: "'Any children born to you after them shall be yours, and they shall be called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit.'"

- Only the first two sons of Joseph received tribal status. Any later sons would be absorbed into the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Ellicott: We gather from Genesis 50:23 that Joseph probably had no other sons; but if he did, they would rank only as heads of families within Ephraim and Manasseh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- The practical result: Joseph's line became two tribes, while each of his eleven brothers had one tribe. This explains why the tribes of Israel can be listed in more than 20 different ways in the Old Testament yet always remain 12 — Levi received no territorial inheritance (being the priestly tribe), and Joseph was divided into two. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

---

## v. 7: "'Now as for me, when I was returning from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died along the way in the land of Canaan… So I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).'"

- Jacob recalls his beloved Rachel, the wife of his affections. Her untimely death prevented her from bearing more sons. By adopting Joseph's two sons, Jacob was honouring Rachel — giving her firstborn a double portion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch: Rachel died "by his side" (*alai* — literally "upon me," i.e., in his arms), without living to see Joseph exalted as the saviour of the whole house of Israel. The adoption of Joseph's sons compensates for her early death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Enduring Word: Jacob mentions this "with lingering grief." Rachel was buried on the road to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19–20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- Ellicott notes the parenthetical "(that is, Bethlehem)" was added later, when Bethlehem had become famous as David's birthplace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 8: "When Israel saw the sons of Joseph, he asked, 'Who are these?'"

- Jacob's eyesight was dim (v. 10), and he may not have seen the youths clearly for some years, so he genuinely did not recognise them. But Ellicott notes the question also serves as "the solemn turning of the discourse to the young men who were now to be invested with patriarchal rank." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch call this the formal opening of the blessing ritual. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 9: "Joseph said to his father, 'They are the sons God has given me in this place.' So Jacob said, 'Please bring them to me, that I may bless them.'"

- Joseph acknowledges God's gift of his sons. The names Manasseh ("forgetfulness") and Ephraim ("fruitfulness") reflected Joseph's experience in Egypt (Genesis 41:51–52). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- The blessing of the dying patriarch was considered irrevocable and carried prophetic weight; this parallels Isaac's blessing of Jacob in Genesis 27. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/genesis/48.htm)

---

## v. 10: "Now Israel's eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see. Joseph brought his sons to him, and his father kissed them and embraced them."

- The physical blindness of Jacob mirrors that of his father Isaac at the time of blessing (Genesis 27:1). But unlike Isaac, who was deceived, Jacob blesses with full spiritual sight — "guiding his hands wittingly." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- Keil & Delitzsch: "The eyes of Israel were heavy with age, so that he could not see well." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 11: "'I never expected to see your face again,' Israel said to Joseph, 'but now God has let me see your children as well.'"

- Jacob expresses joyful astonishment at God's goodness beyond his expectations. He had thought Joseph dead for over 20 years; now he sees not only Joseph but Joseph's sons. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "No choicer favor could fall upon ourselves than to see our children favored of the Lord. Joseph is doubly blessed by seeing Ephraim and Manasseh blessed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

---

## v. 12: "Then Joseph removed his sons from his father's knees and bowed facedown."

- The youths had been between Jacob's knees as he embraced them. Joseph removes them to position them for the formal blessing, then prostrates himself in deep respect. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Ellicott notes some ancient versions (Samaritan, Syriac, LXX) read the verb as a plural, meaning the sons themselves bowed. But the Hebrew pronoun favours the singular — Joseph alone bowed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)

---

## vv. 13–14: Joseph positions his sons — but Jacob crosses his hands.

**v. 13:** "And Joseph took both of them—with Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand—and brought them close to him."

**v. 14:** "But Israel stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head, although Manasseh was the firstborn."

- Joseph deliberately positioned Manasseh (the firstborn) toward Jacob's right hand, so he would receive the right-hand blessing — the position of favour, strength, and preeminence. The right hand throughout Scripture is associated with God's strength (Exodus 15:6), favour (Psalm 16:11), and help (Psalm 20:6). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- Jacob "guided his hands wittingly" (KJV): he knew exactly what he was doing. This was intentional, divinely guided, not a mistake of blindness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** This is the first mention of the laying on of hands in Scripture — a symbolic act by which a spiritual good or gift is transferred. It later appears in ordination (Numbers 27:18, 23), sacrifices, and healings by Christ and the apostles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Cambridge Bible:** "The gesture of benediction, by the laying on of hands, signified the communication of rights and privileges. As in the story of Isaac (ch. 27), the blessing by the head of the house, on his deathbed, was irrevocable." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/genesis/48.htm)
- **Reformed / Ligonier (Calvin):** The Lord purposely changed "the law of nature, to teach us that what he freely confers upon us, is entirely the result of his own will." God owes no one anything; He is free to confer gifts at His own pleasure. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)

---

## vv. 15–16: Jacob's blessing on Ephraim and Manasseh.

**v. 15:** "Then he blessed Joseph and said: 'May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day,'"

**v. 16:** "'the angel who has redeemed me from all harm—may He bless these boys. And may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth.'"

- The text says "he blessed *Joseph*," not the sons — but he blessed Joseph *through* blessing his sons. This identification of the blessing on the father with the blessing on the son illustrates the biblical principle of covenant succession across generations. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)
- **The threefold name of God:** Jacob invokes God under three titles: (1) the God before whom the patriarchs walked; (2) the God who shepherded Jacob; (3) the Angel who redeemed him. Ellicott and Keil & Delitzsch both note that Luther saw this threefold repetition combined with a singular verb ("bless," singular) as a proof of the Trinity in Unity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Luther (cited by Keil & Delitzsch):** "*Non dicit benedicant, pluraliter, nec repetit sed conjungit in uno opere benedicendi tres personas, Deum Patrem, Deum pastorem et Angelum. Sunt igitur hi tres unus Deus et unus benedictor.*" (He does not say 'bless' in the plural, nor does he repeat it, but joins three persons in one act of blessing — God the Father, God the Shepherd, and the Angel. Therefore these three are one God and one Blesser.) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **"The God who has been my shepherd":** The Hebrew is literally "the God who has shepherded me." This is the very first mention in the Bible of God as a shepherd to His people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "The old man's voice faltered as he said, 'The God which fed me all my life long.' The translation would be better if it ran, 'The God which shepherded me all my life long.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **"The Angel who has redeemed me":** This is not a created angel but the Angel of the Lord — the pre-incarnate manifestation of the Messiah (the *Logos*). He is placed on an equality with *Ha-Elohim*. Keil & Delitzsch: "The Angel who is placed on an equality with Ha-Elohim cannot possibly be a created angel, but must be the 'Angel of God,' i.e., God manifested in the form of the Angel of Jehovah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Reformed / Ligonier:** "He is not a creaturely angel, but the angel of the Lord with whom Jacob wrestled (32:22–32), a pre-incarnate manifestation of the Messiah, according to churchmen throughout history." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)
- **Ellicott:** The word *go'el* (redeemer) appears here for the first time in Scripture. It later became the technical term for the nearest kinsman whose duty was to avenge blood; here it is used in the wider sense of a Saviour and Deliverer. Notably, the verb is present tense: "the angel that *redeemeth* me from all evil" — Jacob recognised a continual divine presence guarding him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- **"Let my name be named on them":** Keil & Delitzsch explain this does not simply mean adoption but that "the true nature of the patriarchs shall be discerned and acknowledged in Ephraim and Manasseh" — the blessings of grace and salvation given to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob would be renewed in them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **"Grow into a multitude":** The Hebrew verb *dagah* is related to *dag* (fish), suggesting prolific multiplication like fish. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Spurgeon's sermon on this passage stresses faith:** Jacob's legacies were blessings he possessed "by faith only" — he gave them portions in Canaan, a land not yet possessed. He also notes Jacob's "distinct reference to redemption" — praying that the redeeming Angel would deliver his grandsons "from all evil." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jacob-worshipping-on-his-staff)

---

## vv. 17–18: Joseph objects.

**v. 17:** "When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand on Ephraim's head, he was displeased and took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's."

**v. 18:** "'Not so, my father!' Joseph said. 'This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head.'"

- Joseph assumes his blind father has made a mistake. He intervenes physically, taking hold of Jacob's hand to reposition it according to custom and birth order. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Reformed / Matthew Henry (via Ligonier):** This reminds us that "grace does not observe the order of nature, nor does God prefer those whom we think fittest to be preferred, but as it pleases him." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)

---

## v. 19: "'But his father refused. "I know, my son, I know!" he said. "He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations."'"

- Jacob was not confused; he was acting under divine direction. Both sons would be blessed, but Ephraim would surpass Manasseh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** This prophetic blessing began to be fulfilled from the time of the Judges, when Ephraim took the lead among the northern tribes and became the head of the ten tribes. "Its name acquired equal importance with the name Israel." This was despite Manasseh having 20,000 more fighting men than Ephraim in Moses' census (Numbers 26:34, 37). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Ellicott:** Joshua was an Ephraimite, and after the conquest he held a position comparable to General Washington after American independence — giving his tribe natural preeminence. The ark being placed at Shiloh (in Ephraim) also strengthened the tribe's influence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- **Dummelow:** "Owing to its preeminence the northern kingdom of Israel was often called Ephraim by the prophets." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/genesis-48.html)
- Jeremiah 31:9 later says: "For I am a Father to Israel, and Ephraim is My firstborn." The title "firstborn" in Scripture is often about preeminence, not birth order (e.g., David in Psalm 89:27; Christ in Colossians 1:15). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

---

## v. 20: "'So that day Jacob blessed them and said: "By you shall Israel pronounce this blessing: 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.'" So he put Ephraim before Manasseh.'"

- The blessing became a standing formula in Israel. Ellicott notes: "In conformity with these words, the Israelites to this day use Jacob's formula in blessing their children." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Jewish parents still bless their sons on Sabbath eve with these words: "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh." This is significant because Ephraim and Manasseh were the first brothers in Genesis who lived in harmony — no rivalry, no murder, no deception — making them a model for fraternal peace. (This point is commonly noted in Jewish tradition and some evangelical commentaries.)
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "And thus he placed Ephraim before Manasseh, viz., in the position of his hands and the terms of the blessing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)

---

## v. 21: "Then Israel said to Joseph, 'Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.'"

- This was a passing of the torch. Jacob, the last of the three great patriarchs, expresses firm faith that God would bring his descendants back to Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Enduring Word / Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Traces four stages of spiritual maturity through God's presence language: (1) "I am with you" (Gen 28:15) — assurance for the young believer; (2) "I will be with you" (Gen 31:3) — trust for the growing believer; (3) "God has been with me" (Gen 31:5) — testimony of the mature believer; (4) "God will be with you" (Gen 48:21) — encouragement the mature believer gives to others. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "If Abraham dies, there is Isaac; and if Isaac dies, there is Jacob; and if Jacob dies, there is Joseph… The Lord shall never lack a champion to bear his standard high among the sons of men." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

---

## v. 22: "'And to you, as one who is above your brothers, I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.'"

- **The Hebrew word translated "ridge" or "portion" is *Shechem* (שְׁכֶם),** which also means "shoulder" or "ridge." This is a deliberate wordplay on the town of Shechem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Joseph's bones were later buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32), and John 4:5 refers to "the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph" near Sychar/Shechem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)

### Three main interpretations of "took from the Amorites with my sword and bow":

**1. Prophetic interpretation (most common among conservative commentators):**
- Jacob speaks prophetically, using the perfect tense to describe a future conquest as already accomplished. He did not personally conquer this land, but his descendants would — "by my sword and bow" meaning "by the military conquest of my posterity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch argue this strongly: "Any conquest of territory would have been entirely at variance with the character of the patriarchal history, which consisted in the renunciation of all reliance upon human power." The patriarchs acquired land by purchase, not warfare. The conquest awaited the time when "the iniquity of the Amorites was full" (Genesis 15:16). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)

**2. Literal/historical interpretation:**
- Ellicott suggests it is possible that after the atrocity at Shechem (Genesis 34), the Amorites gathered to avenge the Hivites, and Jacob either deterred them by a show of force or repulsed an actual attack. He notes that "a mighty terror fell upon all the cities round about" (Genesis 35:5) and that Jacob, "a preeminently peaceful and timid man, here alludes to the one military exploit of his life" with exultant spirit. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- Ellicott acknowledges this is a minority view but argues that taking the words "in a non-natural sense" (i.e., purely prophetic) is problematic. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)

**3. Reference to the purchased land at Shechem:**
- Jacob purchased land at Shechem in Genesis 33:19. However, Keil & Delitzsch reject identifying this with that purchase because "a purchase could not possibly be called a conquest by sword and bow." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- Nor can it refer to Simeon and Levi's violent attack on Shechem (Genesis 34), because Jacob cursed that deed (Genesis 49:5–7) and would not claim credit for it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The "Angel" of v. 16 — Who is He?

- **Reformed, Lutheran, and many conservative Evangelicals** (Ligonier, Keil & Delitzsch, Ellicott, Spurgeon): The Angel is the pre-incarnate Christ, the Angel of the LORD, the second Person of the Trinity. Keil & Delitzsch explicitly state that this Angel "cannot possibly be a created angel" because he is placed on an equality with *Ha-Elohim*. Luther saw the threefold name with a singular verb as proof of the Trinity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html) (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Follows the same Trinitarian reading without additional distinctive emphasis. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes):** Same identification — "the Jehovah Angel with whom Jacob wrestled at Jabbok." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-48.html)
- **Methodist/Wesleyan, Anglican:** The traditional commentaries consulted (Ellicott is Anglican) agree with the Trinitarian reading.
- **Summary:** There is no significant disagreement among mainstream Protestant traditions on this point — all identify the Angel as divine, the pre-incarnate Christ or Angel of the LORD.

### The Nature of the Blessing and "Firstborn" Status

- **Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier):** Emphasises sovereign election. God's choice of Ephraim over Manasseh is a "powerful illustration of grace." Calvin: God "owes no one anything, he is free to confer gifts at his own pleasure." This is a key text for the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/josephs-protest)
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Emphasises faith — Jacob blessed "by faith" (Hebrews 11:21), and faith "resolves to do the right thing in the right way… If God will have Ephraim first, faith does not quarrel with his decree." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jacob-worshipping-on-his-staff)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Emphasises the principle that "firstborn" is about preeminence more than birth order, with application to Christ's preeminence and the believer's spiritual growth through stages. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

### The "Ridge of Land" (v. 22) — Did Jacob literally fight?

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Reformed conservative):** Strongly favour the prophetic interpretation — Jacob never personally fought for the land; he spoke prophetically of his descendants' future conquest. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/genesis-48.html)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Allows for the possibility that Jacob did engage in some military action, citing Genesis 35:5 ("a mighty terror fell upon all the cities"). He suggests Jacob may have deterred or repulsed Amorite retaliation after the Shechem massacre. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-48.html)
- **Enduring Word / Guzik:** Simply states that Jacob "battled for control of a portion of land from the Amorites" while still in Canaan and deeded it to Joseph — a straightforward literal reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-48/)

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **Adoption and inheritance:** Jacob adopts Ephraim and Manasseh, giving Joseph the double portion. This explains how Israel can have 13 tribal entities yet always be counted as 12.
2. **God's sovereign choice:** The younger Ephraim is elevated above the elder Manasseh — a recurring pattern in Genesis (Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau) that illustrates grace over natural right.
3. **Trinitarian foreshadowing:** The threefold divine title with a singular verb ("bless") is widely seen across Protestant traditions as a hint of the Trinity.
4. **God as Shepherd:** The first occurrence of this beloved metaphor for God in Scripture.
5. **Faith that looks beyond death:** Jacob blesses with full confidence in promises not yet fulfilled — land not yet possessed, a multitude not yet born. Hebrews 11:21 holds this up as exemplary faith.
